slides.title: Stage-1 Calibration: Procurement and Build
slides.subtitle: The spheres, board and fixtures needed for the depth-sensor calibration captures
slides.notes: This is the first of two decks on the stage-1 calibration captures. It covers what has to be bought and made before a capture session: two matte spheres, a flat board, their mountings on the robot flange, and a three-ball nest, with estimated costs and candidate suppliers. The second deck covers the test procedure itself and what the robot program must do. Both are summaries of the stage-1 capture procedure in docs/procedures, whose section 3a and appendix A hold the full build details.

slides.title: Two spheres and a board carry the known geometry
slides.caption: Sphere on its stem, side view: the stem points away from the sensor so that the sphere hides it.

cards.head: Sphere A
cards.text: 76.2 mm diameter; used from 300 to 550 mm

cards.head: Sphere B
cards.text: 152.4 mm diameter; used from 500 to 1,100 mm

cards.head: Board
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick, flat to 0.05 mm after painting; tilted 0, 20 and 40 degrees

slides.notes: The calibration compares what the sensor measures with targets of known shape held at known poses by the robot. Two sphere sizes are used because the bias from averaging over a curved surface depends on curvature; two radii a factor of two apart let the correction map carry curvature as an input and remove that bias. Both spheres are used around 500 to 550 mm so the two radii overlap. The board supplies zero curvature and controlled tilts. A sphere's orientation does not matter, only its center, which is why the mounting must hold the center fixed rather than aim the sphere precisely.

slides.title: New equipment costs about $1,900 to $5,400

rows: Sphere A, bearing ball, bonded stem, blasted, measured
Sphere B, turned aluminum, anodized, measured
Board, glass or ground aluminum, painted

stats.label: bearing-ball sphere A, aluminum sphere B

slides.caption: Estimates of October 2026, plus or minus 50 percent; sphere B is the least certain. The sensor, robot and capture computer are in hand.
slides.notes: These estimates come from suppliers' list prices where they exist and from typical job-shop rates of about 80 to 150 dollars an hour otherwise. The sphere figures include 100 to 300 dollars for having the diameter measured at a calibration laboratory. The two totals differ only in the spheres: a bearing ball with a bonded stem and a turned aluminum sphere, against both spheres made to order by a ball or ceramics maker. Quotes are needed before ordering, and the sphere choice itself is still open, pending a canvass of the market.

slides.title: Spheres must be matte and measured, not certified

columns.head: Finish
points: Every bearing ball arrives mirror-bright: unusable
Bead-blast with fine glass bead: removes micrometers
Matte paint is second choice: 0.02 to 0.05 mm per coat
"Chrome steel" is the 52100 alloy, not plating

columns.head: Diameter
points: Known to 0.025 mm, measured after the finish
Micrometer at several orientations, or a CMM
Aluminum grows 0.0035 mm per degree C: measure at session temperature
The measured value goes in the pose log

columns.head: Mounting
points: Hardened balls cannot be tapped
Steel ball: drilled or EDM blind hole, bonded stem
Aluminum sphere B: thread cut when it is turned
No pre-tapped precision sphere exists above 1.5 inch

slides.notes: A mirror finish returns one bright highlight from the sensor's projector and almost nothing else, so every sphere must be made matte. Bead-blasting is preferred because it changes the diameter by only micrometers. The diameter requirement is decision D-13: known to 0.025 mm after finishing, which is a radius error of about 0.0125 mm, an eighth of the target at 500 mm; no maker's certificate is needed. CMM means coordinate measuring machine and EDM means electrical discharge machining. Bearing-grade balls are hardened to about 60 HRC and cannot be tapped afterwards, which is why steel spheres get a bonded stem.

slides.title: Candidate suppliers

rows: Bal-tec; RGP Balls; Industrial Tectonics; Morgan Advanced Materials
3 and 6 inch matte spheres with a mounting hole are custom items
MetrologyWorks up to 1.5 inch; Rothbucher 145 mm, sphericity 0.3 mm
McMaster-Carr MIC-6 plus a grinding shop; Edmund Optics float glass
Painted matte after grinding; flatness checked after mounting
Local machine shop; EDM shop for hardened balls
Calibration laboratory with a coordinate measuring machine

slides.caption: From suppliers' web pages, October 2026; not an endorsement. Confirm size, finish, measurement and thread before ordering.
slides.notes: This list is appendix A of the procedure in brief. No supplier was found that stocks a precision sphere of the needed sizes with a mounting hole, so the spheres are either made to order or built from a bearing ball by a machine shop. The laser-scanner reference spheres sold in the right sizes generally have form errors of 0.5 to 2 mm, far too coarse; the Rothbucher sphere is the best specified of them. A calibration laboratory measures the finished diameters, which is cheaper than buying certified spheres and is what the calibration actually needs.

slides.title: A stiff, repeatable chain from flange to sphere
slides.caption: Adapter on the flange's dowel, with the stem's shoulder seated on the adapter face.
points: Adapter located by the flange dowel, so a remount lands in the same place
Ground stem, 16 mm for A and 30 mm for B, keeps sag to 0.02 to 0.05 mm
Stem length at least 2R + 50 mm, so the sphere hides the stem
Witness mark across stem and adapter shows a loosened joint
After any remount, re-check in the nest: readings within 0.1 mm
slides.notes: Where the sphere center ends up does not need to be known from drawings, because the tool-center-point routine measures it; what matters is that it does not move afterwards. The adapter plate's mounting face, outer face and tapped hole are machined in one lathe setup, located on the flange pilot, so the hole is perpendicular to the face within 0.02 mm over 100 mm. The stems are deliberately thick: a 12 mm stem would let sphere A sag about 0.07 mm, and that sag would change with the robot's orientation. The shoulder on the stem, machined square in the same setup as its thread, sets the stem perpendicular to the adapter.

slides.title: The sphere end: threaded insert or bonded stem
slides.label: Ceramic sphere: maker's threaded insert
slides.caption: The hole need not be exactly radial: the tool-center-point routine measures the center wherever it ends up.
slides.notes: Precision ceramic spheres are sold with a threaded insert bonded in by the maker; the stem tip is turned to a matching thread with a small shoulder that seats on the flat around the insert, with a drop of medium-strength thread locker. Bearing-grade steel balls are hardened to about 60 HRC and cannot be tapped, so a shop makes a blind hole about 0.6 R deep by carbide drilling or electrical discharge machining, sized for a light press fit, and the stem is bonded in with anaerobic retaining compound. Never weld or braze: the heat distorts the sphere. A turned aluminum sphere B can have the stem thread cut into it when it is made.

slides.title: The board must stay flat after finishing and mounting
slides.caption: Board on its adapter. The runout and frame checks shown here are done at setup (deck 2).

cards.head: Plate
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick; ground aluminum tooling plate or float glass

cards.head: Finish
cards.text: Matte light gray paint on the front face; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm, it bows

cards.head: Flatness
cards.text: 0.05 mm, checked after painting and mounting, not before; keep the flatness report

cards.head: Adapter
cards.text: Two dowels and a clamp hold the board square to the flange axis, centered on it, and in the same place after a remount

slides.notes: Thickness is not a stiffness question: a 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight. It only has to survive the finish and the mounting flat. Bead-blasting peens one face and bows a thin plate, so paint over the ground or glass surface instead. Flatness is checked last, after painting and mounting, because that is the state the sensor sees; the flatness report is also the reference for the board-flatness check in the validation.

slides.title: A three-ball nest holds each sphere at a fixed center
points: Three hardened balls, about 24 mm diameter, pressed into a base
Ordinary grade-25 bearing balls are good enough: the nest's quality comes from the balls being rigidly fixed
Bolted to the table where the robot reaches with the wrist down and tilted about 40 degrees to either side
Used once per sphere at setup, and after any remount of an adapter or stem
slides.notes: A sphere resting on three fixed balls always has its center at the same point in space, whatever direction its stem points. That is what lets the robot's own multi-orientation routine find the sphere's center as its tool center point, which deck 2 describes. The nest is simple to make: a steel base with three pockets, the balls pressed in, and holes to bolt it down. Its position matters only in that the robot must be able to seat the sphere from several directions.

slides.title: Checks before the fixtures go to the robot cell
checklist: Adapter tapped hole square to its mounting face within 0.02 mm over 100 mm
Each stem straight: roll it on a flat surface
Both spheres matte, uniform and free of highlights
Each sphere diameter measured after finishing, with the temperature recorded
Board flat to 0.05 mm after painting and mounting
Witness marks across each stem-adapter joint
Robot payload rating covers sphere, stem and adapter together
slides.notes: These are the build checks scattered through section 3a of the procedure, gathered in one place. Each one protects something the software cannot repair later: a crooked or bending stem moves the sphere center away from the measured tool center point, a shiny spot gives bad reads, and an unmeasured diameter or a bowed board puts a wrong reference into every observation.
